title: How to Achieve More in Less Time
author: Elevated Path
summary: This newsletter applies the Pareto Principle, popularised by management thinker Joseph Juran, to personal productivity. Its premise is that most people have a priority problem rather than a time problem, because a small number of activities produce a disproportionate share of results. It lays out a seven-step process: define a specific outcome, list everything you do, identify what actually produces results, isolate the vital few, double down on them, reduce the low-impact remainder, and re-evaluate regularly. The author stresses that the 80/20 split is illustrative and that the real point is unequal contribution. A section on the productivity trap warns that being busy is not the same as making progress and that impact, not activity, is the goal. The piece closes with a repeating loop of define, list, measure, identify, double down, reduce, and repeat.
points: Most productivity problems are priority problems, since a few activities generate most of the outcomes you care about.
Start by defining a specific, measurable result, because you cannot find your most valuable activities without knowing what you are improving.
Rank activities by what they produce rather than the effort they take, then split them into the vital few and the useful many.
Double down on proven high-leverage work and cut or shrink the low-value bottom 80 percent, while keeping some room for experimentation.
Revisit your vital few every few weeks because what produces results today may stop working as conditions change.
quotes: Most people don’t have a time problem. They have a priority problem.
A small number of causes often produce a large share of the results. The numbers don’t have to be exactly 80% and 20%. The important idea is unequal contribution.
The goal isn’t to blindly assume that everything follows an exact 80/20 split. The goal is to ask: “Which few things are creating most of the outcome I care about?
Stop looking at how much effort something requires. Look at what it produces.
You can spend eight hours working and accomplish less than someone who spends three hours on the right thing. Because time spent is not the same as value created.
Your 20% isn’t permanent. What works today might stop working tomorrow.
The Pareto Principle isn’t about doing less work. It’s about doing less of what doesn’t matter and more of what actually moves the needle.
